title: Sexually Explicit Deepfake Sites Target 100-Plus Politicians in Europe
gist: New research by Benjamin Shultz (Agora Digitale Transformation / American Sunlight Project) analyzing 160 deepfake-abuse domains found 138 of roughly 5,800 European national MPs appeared on the sites versus only 9 men, a 33x gender skew, prompting new UK/EU nudify-service bans and US Take It Down Act takedowns.

themes.theme: Scale and gender skew of the deepfake targeting

insights.claim: Researcher Benjamin Shultz's analysis of approximately 160 domains hosting deepfake abuse and nonconsensual sexual content found that at least 138 women members of parliament from 22 EU countries appeared or were mentioned on the sites, versus only 9 male MPs — making women MPs 33 times more likely to be targeted, based on a compiled database of more than 5,800 European national MPs.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: A quantified 33x gender disparity in deepfake targeting of sitting politicians gives regulators and platforms a hard benchmark for assessing the scale of gendered AI-enabled harassment, likely to be cited in upcoming EU/UK legislative debates.
insights.quote: By Shultz's calculations, it is 33 times more likely for women MPs to be targeted by deepfake ecosystems.

insights.claim: Politicians from Germany, the Netherlands, Italy, and France appeared most frequently on the deepfake websites, and more senior politicians were more likely to be targeted, according to the research.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Targeting correlates with seniority and specific national political systems, suggesting deepfake abuse tracks visibility/prominence rather than random distribution — useful for prioritizing platform enforcement and national legislative response.
insights.quote: Politicians from Germany, the Netherlands, Italy, and France appeared on the websites the most, according to the findings, and the more senior a politician is, the more likely they were to be targeted.

insights.claim: The deepfake sites host multiple categories of abusive content, including actively hosted explicit videos, indexed results of removed content, and 'gateway' profile pages listing an MP's name, official photo, and personal/social media details alongside direct links to 'nudifier' apps, meaning a user can generate new nonconsensual imagery of a named politician in as few as three clicks.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess (citing Benjamin Shultz)
insights.so_what: Frictionless three-click generation pipelines from a public profile page to a working nudify tool illustrate why platform-level enforcement (blocking gateway pages, not just hosted content) is the more effective intervention point.
insights.quote: It has all the images, all the information, and a direct link to the tool, and in three clicks you can generate... That's just as bad as actually hosting the content.

themes.theme: Business model of the deepfake ecosystem

insights.claim: AI adviser and deepfake expert Henry Ajder, who has tracked the deepfake ecosystem since 2018, describes these platforms as designed and operated 'like businesses,' with infrastructure built to enable abusive content generation at scale and with ease.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess (citing Henry Ajder)
insights.so_what: Framing deepfake abuse sites as commercial operations (not just isolated bad actors) implies revenue models, hosting/payment infrastructure, and supply chains that could be targeted via financial and infrastructure-level enforcement, not just content takedowns.
insights.quote: These platforms are designed to run like businesses... The whole infrastructure is set up to do this at scale with ease.

insights.claim: Since AI-generated deepfakes first emerged at the end of 2017, the underlying technology has become significantly more accessible and realistic over time, and millions of nonconsensual AI images and videos have since been created, mostly by men and boys, used to harass, intimidate, or blackmail women and girls — including incidents at nearly 100 schools worldwide.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: The trajectory from 2017 emergence to millions of images and school-level incidents at ~100 schools shows the harm has scaled from novelty to systemic societal problem within roughly nine years, informing urgency for regulatory intervention.
insights.quote: Over time, millions of nonconsensual AI images and videos have been created, mostly by men and boys, and are often used to harass, intimidate, or blackmail women and girls, including at almost 100 schools around the world.

insights.claim: Researchers and lawmakers argue that deepfake targeting of politicians can produce a chilling effect that discourages women and girls from entering or remaining in public life, causing both immediate psychological damage and long-term reputational harm even after they leave politics.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess (citing Benjamin Shultz)
insights.so_what: A documented causal link between deepfake abuse and women's withdrawal from public office is a democratic-participation risk that legislators are already citing to justify new nudify-service bans.
insights.quote: This discourages women from taking office in the first place and also crowds these women out of public life... There's so much evidence to support that this does real psychological damage.

insights.claim: Dutch MPs Suzanne Kröger and Sarah Dobbe, both personally affected, describe the deepfake content as part of a broader pattern of online hate and intimidation targeting women and female politicians, and call for faster content removal and direct victim support.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess (citing Suzanne Kröger and Sarah Dobbe)
insights.so_what: First-person accounts from sitting MPs personally affected lend political weight and urgency to legislative responses already underway in the Netherlands and EU.
insights.quote: Deepfake porn is part of a much bigger trend of online hate and intimidation against women and female politicians.
insights.locator: Kröger quote near top of article

themes.theme: Enforcement and legislative response is accelerating

insights.claim: Both the UK and EU are planning bans on 'nudify' services (AI tools that digitally undress people in photos), and under the US Take It Down Act, at least two major deepfake websites publishing thousands of celebrity images and videos have already been taken offline.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Concrete legislative action (UK/EU nudify bans, US Take It Down Act enforcement) signals a fast-moving regulatory crackdown that will affect AI companies and platforms offering or hosting image-generation tools, raising compliance risk for AI vendors with lax content controls.
insights.quote: Both the UK and EU are planning bans on nudify services, while under the US Take It Down Act, at least two major deepfake websites publishing thousands of images and videos of celebrities have been taken offline.

insights.claim: Ahead of this story's publication, Wired found that at least half a dozen of the domains identified in the research had recently been removed from the web, reducing the total number of depictions of European MPs, and Shultz's earlier 2024 research on US senators/Congress members showed a 'significant decrease' in depictions after those sites were taken down.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess (citing Benjamin Shultz)
insights.so_what: Empirical evidence that takedown enforcement measurably reduces deepfake depictions (both in the new EU research and Shultz's prior 2024 US Congress study) validates takedown-focused enforcement as an effective, if incomplete, mitigation strategy.
insights.quote: After the websites were taken down, Shultz says, there has been a 'significant decrease' in the number of depictions of those American politicians that appeared on the websites two years ago.
